parts.title: Joining a community choir
parts.context: A woman phones the secretary of a community choir to ask about joining.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Part 1. You will hear a woman phoning the secretary of a community choir. First, you have some time to look at questions 1 to 5.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: You will see that there is an example that has been done for you. On this occasion only, the conversation relating to this will be played first.

script.speaker: martin
script.text: Hello, Northfield Choir, Martin speaking.

script.speaker: grace
script.text: Hi, I saw your poster in the library, and I'd like to know more about joining the choir. When do you meet?

script.speaker: martin
script.text: We rehearse every Tuesday evening, all year except August.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: The choir rehearses on Tuesdays, so 'Tuesday' has been written in the space. Now we shall begin. You should answer the questions as you listen, because you will not hear the recording a second time. Listen carefully and answer questions 1 to 5.

script.speaker: grace
script.text: And where are the rehearsals?

script.speaker: martin
script.text: In the hall at Saint Anne's School, on Park Road. We perform in Saint Anne's Church, which is next door, so people sometimes get confused, but rehearsals are always in the school.

script.speaker: grace
script.text: And how long do they last?

script.speaker: martin
script.text: We start at half past seven and finish at half past nine, so two hours, with a short break for tea in the middle.

script.speaker: grace
script.text: Is there a fee?

script.speaker: martin
script.text: It's sixty pounds a term. Students pay half, so thirty.

script.speaker: grace
script.text: I'm not a student, I'm a nurse, so sixty. That's fine. Now, I'm a bit worried, because I've never read music.

script.speaker: martin
script.text: Oh, don't worry about that. You don't need to be able to read music at all. Most of our members learn the songs by ear.

script.speaker: grace
script.text: That's a relief. Is there an audition?

script.speaker: martin
script.text: Not really. It's just a short chat with the conductor, so she can find out which part suits your voice.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Before you hear the rest of the conversation, you have some time to look at questions 6 to 10.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Now listen and answer questions 6 to 10.

script.speaker: grace
script.text: What's the conductor's name?

script.speaker: martin
script.text: Delia Hartwell. That's H-A-R-T-W-E-L-L. She's been with us for ten years.

script.speaker: grace
script.text: And when's your next concert?

script.speaker: martin
script.text: We usually have one in November, but this year the cathedral was booked, so the next concert is in December. It'll be a Christmas programme.

script.speaker: grace
script.text: Lovely. Do I need to buy anything?

script.speaker: martin
script.text: Everyone uses a black folder for their music, so that the choir looks neat on stage. You can buy one from us for five pounds.

script.speaker: grace
script.text: OK. Anything I should bring each week?

script.speaker: martin
script.text: Always bring a pencil. Delia makes a lot of changes, and you'll need to mark them in your music.

script.speaker: grace
script.text: And is there parking at the school?

script.speaker: martin
script.text: Not much, I'm afraid. Most people park in the supermarket car park opposite. It's free after six.

script.speaker: grace
script.text: Perfect. I'll see you on Tuesday, then.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: That is the end of Part 1. You now have half a minute to check your answers.

parts.title: Volunteering at a wildlife rescue centre
parts.context: The manager of a wildlife rescue centre talks to a group of new volunteers.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Part 2. You will hear the manager of a wildlife rescue centre talking to new volunteers. First, you have some time to look at questions 11 to 15.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions 11 to 15.

script.speaker: dan
script.text: Hi, everyone, and welcome to Hollybrook Wildlife Rescue. I'm Dan, the manager. Let's start with a quick look at the map, so you know your way around. We're standing at the entrance, at the bottom of the map, and Reception is the building on your right.

script.speaker: dan
script.text: Immediately on your left as you come in is the food store. That's where you'll collect the food for each animal at the start of your shift, so you'll be visiting it a lot.

script.speaker: dan
script.text: If you walk up the main path to the crossroads and turn right, then right at the far end of that path is the hedgehog unit. It's kept well away from the entrance because hedgehogs are easily stressed by noise.

script.speaker: dan
script.text: If you turn left at the crossroads instead, and keep going past the pond, you'll come to the bird hospital, right at the end of the path.

script.speaker: dan
script.text: Going straight on at the crossroads, the first building on your right, just before the woodland, is the owl barn. Please keep your voice down when you go past.

script.speaker: dan
script.text: And where the main path ends, at the very top of the map, are the release pens. That's where animals spend their last few days, getting used to life outside before we set them free.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Before you hear the rest of the talk, you have some time to look at questions 16 to 20.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Now listen and answer questions 16 to 20.

script.speaker: dan
script.text: Now, some rules. People often think the hardest rule is not giving the animals names, and it is hard. But the one rule that matters most is washing your hands before and after you touch any animal. Some of their diseases can pass to people, and the other way round.

script.speaker: dan
script.text: You might expect us to be full of foxes, and in spring we do get a lot of baby birds. But over the whole year, hedgehogs are by far our most common patients.

script.speaker: dan
script.text: On your first day, you won't handle any animals or prepare their food. You'll be cleaning out the enclosures with an experienced volunteer, which is a great way to learn how everything works.

script.speaker: dan
script.text: Why do we need so many new volunteers this year? We always lose a few to university in the autumn, but that's normal. The real reason is that we're now taking in almost twice as many animals as we did five years ago.

script.speaker: dan
script.text: And finally, if a member of the public arrives with an injured animal, please don't take it from them yourself. Ask them to fill in a form at Reception, so we know exactly where the animal was found. We always try to release animals back in the place they came from.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: That is the end of Part 2. You now have half a minute to check your answers.

parts.title: A presentation on fast fashion
parts.context: Two students prepare a presentation about the environmental cost of cheap clothing.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Part 3. You will hear two students, Ella and Noah, preparing a presentation about fast fashion. First, you have some time to look at questions 21 to 25.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions 21 to 25.

script.speaker: noah
script.text: So, Ella, why did you want to do fast fashion? Is it because you work in a clothes shop?

script.speaker: ella
script.text: I do work in one on Saturdays, but that's not really why. It was when I sorted out my wardrobe and realised how many things I'd only worn once. I wanted to change my own habits, and I thought the research would help.

script.speaker: noah
script.text: Fair enough. Now, sources. I like the charity's website, it's very clear.

script.speaker: ella
script.text: It is, but it's quite one-sided. And the government report is six years old. I think the university study should be our main source. It's the most recent, and they explain exactly how they collected the data.

script.speaker: noah
script.text: Agreed. You know, I knew that making clothes uses a lot of water. What really shocked me was that less than one percent of old clothing is recycled into new clothes.

script.speaker: ella
script.text: I know, it's terrible. What about the practical part? We said we'd do a survey of our class.

script.speaker: noah
script.text: Two other groups are already doing surveys. Why don't we organise a clothes swap instead? People bring things they don't wear, and take something new home.

script.speaker: ella
script.text: I love that. Let's do it. And one more thing. I looked at our draft slides again last night, and they've got far too much text. People will read instead of listening to us.

script.speaker: noah
script.text: True. Let's cut them down to a few words each and use more pictures.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Before you hear the rest of the discussion, you have some time to look at questions 26 to 30.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Now listen and answer questions 26 to 30.

script.speaker: ella
script.text: We should end with some possible solutions. Buying second-hand clothes, first.

script.speaker: noah
script.text: That's already really popular with people our age. The selling apps have made it so easy.

script.speaker: ella
script.text: Then renting clothes. It's a nice idea, but the prices mean only quite rich people can actually do it.

script.speaker: noah
script.text: Repairing clothes is good, but most people don't even know how to sew on a button any more. That should be taught in schools again.

script.speaker: ella
script.text: What about a tax on fast fashion?

script.speaker: noah
script.text: People would hate it, but honestly, I think it would change people's behaviour more than anything else on our list.

script.speaker: ella
script.text: And labels showing the environmental cost of each item? It sounds simple, but measuring the impact of every single item would be very hard to actually do.

script.speaker: noah
script.text: Good. That gives us a strong ending.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: That is the end of Part 3. You now have half a minute to check your answers.

parts.title: Lecture: the science of concert hall acoustics
parts.context: A lecture on how scientists learned to design rooms where music sounds good.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Part 4. You will hear a lecture about the acoustics of concert halls. First, you have some time to look at questions 31 to 40.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions 31 to 40.

script.speaker: lecturer
script.text: Good morning. Today we're looking at acoustics, the science of how sound behaves in a room, and in particular how it changed the design of concert halls.

script.speaker: lecturer
script.text: Our story begins in eighteen ninety-five at Harvard University, which had just opened a new lecture hall. There was a serious problem: students could not understand the lecturers, because every word echoed around the room. In fact, a single word could be heard for more than five seconds.

script.speaker: lecturer
script.text: The university asked a young physicist, Wallace Sabine, to solve the problem. He needed a material that would soak up sound, so, late at night, he and his assistants borrowed hundreds of seat cushions from a theatre nearby, carried them into the hall, and measured how each extra cushion changed the sound. Every morning, they had to return the cushions before the theatre opened.

script.speaker: lecturer
script.text: After years of measurements, Sabine discovered a simple rule. How long a sound lasts in a room depends on two things: the volume of the room, and how much sound its surfaces absorb. For the first time, architects could predict how a room would sound before it was built.

script.speaker: lecturer
script.text: His great test came with Symphony Hall in Boston, which opened in nineteen hundred. It was the first concert hall in the world to be designed using science rather than guesswork, and it's still considered one of the best.

script.speaker: lecturer
script.text: Symphony Hall is long, high and narrow, a design that's often called a shoebox. Narrow halls work well because sound bounces off the side walls and reaches the audience from both sides, which listeners find very pleasing.

script.speaker: lecturer
script.text: Even the decoration has a job to do. The statues and carvings on the walls scatter the sound in many directions, so that it spreads evenly around the hall.

script.speaker: lecturer
script.text: In nineteen sixty-three, the Philharmonie in Berlin broke with tradition. Instead of putting the orchestra at one end, the architect placed the orchestra in the middle, with the audience sitting all around it on terraces, rather like a vineyard on a hillside.

script.speaker: lecturer
script.text: And modern halls go further still. Many can change their acoustics for different kinds of music, using moving panels in the ceiling and heavy curtains that can be lowered to absorb more sound.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: That is the end of Part 4. You now have half a minute to check your answers.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: That is the end of the Listening test.
